name: Ultherapy / HIFU skin tightening
lead: Ultherapy is a non-invasive cosmetic procedure that uses micro-focused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) to heat deep skin layers, with the aim of lifting and tightening skin on areas such as the brow, neck and under the chin. It is made by Ulthera, Inc., which Merz Aesthetics acquired in 2014.[1] Other devices using high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) for skin tightening are sold under different names.

For someone looking to look younger without surgery, the appeal is that the energy is delivered below the skin surface, so there is no incision and, per the manufacturer, little or no downtime. The heat is said to prompt the skin to build new collagen and elastin over the following months, producing a gradual lift of the brow, a firmer jawline and neck, and smoother chest skin.[1][12]

The device received its first FDA clearance in 2009 for non-invasive eyebrow lifting, with later clearances for the neck and under-chin area in 2012 and for lines and wrinkles on the decolletage in 2014.[1] In November 2025 the FDA cleared the newer Ultherapy PRIME system for skin laxity on the arms and abdomen.[12]

Evidence for skin tightening comes mainly from small device trials. One summary of pooled data reports investigator-rated improvement of about 92 percent at 90 days, while patient-reported satisfaction ranged from roughly 42 to 59 percent.[1] That summary relies partly on clinic and manufacturer material.

paras: Focused ultrasound creates small zones of thermal coagulation in the dermis and in the deeper SMAS layer while sparing the surface epidermis. The resulting heat injury is said to trigger a healing response that produces new collagen and elastin, and ultrasound imaging lets the clinician place the energy at chosen depths.[1] General reviews of HIFU describe it as a technique for non-invasive tissue heating, used far more widely in tumour ablation than in cosmetics.[2][3]

The physics is general to focused ultrasound: several beams converge on a small spot, so tissue at the focus can reach roughly 65 to 85 degrees Celsius and coagulate, while tissue along the beam path stays cooler. Heated regions are small, on the order of a few millimetres, so larger areas are treated by many repeated sonications.[11]

Cleared uses listed for the system include lifting the eyebrow, tightening skin of the neck and under the chin, and improving lines and wrinkles on the decolletage, with arms and abdomen added for the PRIME platform.[1][12] The manufacturer says the treatment is done in a single session in the clinic and that results last up to 12 months on the face and at least 6 months on the arms and abdomen.[12]

The Grokipedia summary describes results appearing over about 2 to 6 months and notes that repeat treatment is common.[1] Practitioners and manufacturers promote it as an option for people who want some lifting but are not seeking surgical results.

Ulthera was founded in 2004 as a spin-off from Guided Therapy Systems and grew from HIFU research in the late 1990s and early 2000s. The company reports one million treatments by 2017 and more than three million by 2025, and launched the PRIME platform in 2024.[1] Merz Aesthetics cited more than 3.5 million treatments worldwide in its 2025 announcement.[12]

Therapeutic focused ultrasound itself has a longer history in medicine: it was explored for neurological disorders in the 1940s, and the first MRI-guided focused ultrasound system received FDA market approval in 2009.[11]

Reported results appear gradually over months. Evidence for body areas such as the abdomen and arms is described as mostly pilot data.[1] Manufacturer material cites patient satisfaction of 95 percent across the Ultherapy line, while the pooled figures summarised above show a lower range for patient-reported satisfaction than for investigator ratings.[1][12]

Common effects are redness, swelling, tenderness, pain and tingling or numbness. Less common effects include bruising, prolonged numbness and temporary facial weakness. Burns and fat atrophy have been reported mostly in post-marketing surveillance, and one small study reported a 23 percent complication rate.[1] Open wounds and implants in the treatment area are listed as contraindications.[1]

Registered small device studies include trials in neck lifting (n=18), the ageing hand (n=7), acne scars (n=20), upper inner arm laxity (n=15), a brow-lift and face-and-neck study of the Octave system (n=50), decolletage wrinkles (n=99), surgical scars, spider veins and gene expression after treatment.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10] The registry listings do not themselves report outcomes.

card.summary: Clinic ultrasound device cleared for brow, neck and chest lifting; modest, gradual results and mostly small device studies.
card.note: Results are reported to last 1 to 2 years; burns and fat atrophy are rare reported events.

quick.overview:
Ultherapy uses focused ultrasound to heat deep skin layers so that skin looks lifted over the following months. It was first FDA cleared in 2009 for brow lifting, later for the neck, chin and chest.

Studies are mostly small device trials; reported improvement is gradual and typically lasts one to two years.
quick.mechanism: Focused ultrasound creates tiny heat zones in the dermis and SMAS layer with imaging guidance, said to prompt new collagen and elastin over time.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, swelling, pain and tingling. Rarer reports include bruising, numbness, temporary facial weakness, burns and fat atrophy. It is done by trained clinicians.

chain: Focused ultrasound heats small zones in the dermis and deeper SMAS layer
Healing response is said to build new collagen and elastin
Gradual lift of brow, jawline, neck and chest over 2 to 6 months
angle.text: Ultherapy is chosen by people who want a firmer, lifted look on the brow, jaw, neck or chest without surgery. Results build gradually over months and, per the manufacturer, last up to about a year on the face.
